findings.trigger_condition: Two nodes where one is hashable and the other is unhashable, but they are __eq__ equal. Example: frozenset({1,2}) as one node and {1,2} (set) as another. Python evaluates frozenset({1,2}) == {1,2} as True, but the code assigns them different IDs because hashable values go through hash_buckets (line 42) while unhashable values go through unhashable_ids/unhashable_nodes (line 44-52), and these two paths never cross-compare.
findings.root_cause: _id_of partitions the node universe into two disjoint lookup domains: hash_buckets for hashable values and unhashable_ids/unhashable_nodes for unhashable values. When a new hashable value arrives, it is only compared against other hashable values in hash_buckets (lines 53-56). When an unhashable value arrives, it is only compared against other unhashable values (lines 44-46). No cross-boundary comparison ever occurs. This means two values A (hashable) and B (unhashable) where A == B will receive different integer IDs and be treated as distinct nodes throughout the algorithm.
findings.impact: Incorrect graph topology: two logically identical nodes are split into separate vertices. This can cause (1) a self-loop (a, a-equivalent) to be silently treated as a 2-node acyclic chain instead of raising DependencyCycleError, (2) spurious extra layers or misplaced nodes in the output, and (3) violation of the contract's first-appearance ordering guarantee since the 'same' node now appears in two different positions. Concrete reproducer: dependency_layers([(frozenset({1,2}), {1,2})]) returns [[{1,2}], [frozenset({1,2})]] (2 layers, 2 different nodes) instead of raising DependencyCycleError for the self-loop.
findings.suggested_validation: Test with edges = [(frozenset({1,2}), {1,2})]. Expected: DependencyCycleError (self-loop on a single node). Actual: returns 2-layer result with no error. Also test with a custom HashableWrapper class whose __eq__ returns True when compared to a list — same silent split occurs.

findings.trigger_condition: Any hashable value used as a node. The hash_buckets dict is keyed by the value itself (line 42: hash_buckets.setdefault(value, [])), not by hash(value). Python's dict already groups keys by hash + __eq__, so each dict entry corresponds to exactly one equality class. The bucket list (list[int]) stored as the dict value will therefore never contain more than one element.
findings.root_cause: The code's naming and structure (hash_buckets, a dict mapping to lists of IDs, with a linear scan loop on lines 53-56) suggests the author intended open-addressing/chaining for hash collisions. But since the dict key is the value itself — not hash(value) — Python's dict handles collision resolution internally. Each dict entry maps one equality class to one bucket list. The bucket is always length 0 (new value, after setdefault creates it) or length 1 (existing value). The for-loop on lines 53-56 is dead complexity: it always executes exactly 0 or 1 iterations.
findings.impact: No correctness bug — the code produces correct results for the hashable-only path. However, the unnecessary list indirection (setdefault creates a list, append adds to it, for-loop scans it) adds constant-factor overhead per _id_of call. More importantly, the misleading 'bucket' abstraction obscures the code's actual O(1) amortized behavior and makes the cross-hashability bug (F1) harder to spot during review, since the structure suggests hash-collision handling is the code's responsibility rather than Python's.
findings.suggested_validation: Instrument _id_of to log len(bucket) after each call. Verify it never exceeds 1, confirming the for-loop is always a single-iteration or zero-iteration pass. Alternatively, replace the entire hash_buckets + bucket-list structure with a plain dict[value, int] (direct value-to-ID mapping) and confirm all tests still pass.

findings.trigger_condition: Graph with many unhashable nodes (e.g., lists). For U unhashable unique nodes across E edges, each _id_of call on an unhashable value performs a linear scan of unhashable_nodes (line 44-46), giving O(U) per lookup and O(U * E) total for unhashable node registration.
findings.root_cause: The unhashable fallback path (lines 44-46) uses a linear scan: `for idx, candidate in zip(unhashable_ids, unhashable_nodes): if candidate is value or candidate == value`. There is no indexing structure for unhashable values — each new lookup must scan all previously registered unhashable nodes. This is inherently O(U) per call where U is the number of unique unhashable nodes.
findings.impact: Quadratic time complexity for graphs composed entirely of unhashable nodes. Empirically verified: 2000 unhashable nodes in a chain takes 0.158s, 4000 takes 0.642s — a 4x increase for 2x input, confirming O(n²). For typical dependency graphs with mostly hashable nodes (strings, ints) this is negligible, but adversarial or unusual inputs (nodes are dicts, lists, or sets) will degrade. The TASKS.md contract does not specify a complexity requirement, so this is a performance concern rather than a contract violation.
findings.suggested_validation: Benchmark with N unhashable nodes in a linear chain for N = 1000, 2000, 4000, 8000. Plot time vs N. Expect quadratic growth confirming O(N²) in the unhashable path. Compare with a version that uses id()-based dict for unhashable identity dedup (O(1) amortized) with a separate equality scan only for distinct-identity-but-equal-value dedup.
